title: RoPA, 1951
lead: Are our election laws resilient enough to defend the ==spirit of democracy, not just its ritual==? The answer lies not only in how we enforce the law, but in how we reform it — transforming it from a ==reactive mechanism into a proactive bulwark== of democratic ethics.

items.title: s.8 — Conviction-Based
bullets: ==If only fined==: from date of conviction; ==if jailed==: from release

==Irrespective of punishment== — Civil Rights Act 1955, Customs Act 1962, ==UAPA 1967==, NDPS 1985, Religious Institutions 1988, ==Places of Worship Act 1991==, National Honour Act 1971, Sati (Prevention) Act 1988, ==Corruption Act 1988==; some BNS offences (promoting enmity, bribery, rape, cruelty); some ==electoral offences== (booth capturing, ballot tampering)
==Minimum 6 months' jail== — hoarding/profiteering/adulteration of food or drugs; ==Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961==
==Any other law: minimum 2 years' jail==

items.title: ss.8A–10A — Other Grounds
bullets: ==s.8A==: convicted for ==‘corrupt practices’ under s.123== (bribery, undue influence, coercion) — President decides on ECI advice based on a court finding; order presented ==within 3 months==; ==max 6-year ban==
==s.9==: ==5-year== disqualification if dismissed for ==disloyalty or corruption== (ECI → President/Governor)
==s.9A==: disqualified ==so long as== the member holds ==commercial contracts with the Union/State==
==s.10==: disqualified while a ==Manager or Agent of a company 25% owned by Union/State== (except cooperative societies)
==s.10A==: ==3-year== disqualification for ==improperly filed election expenses==

head: Aspect
Corrupt practices
Electoral offences
rows: Only if specifically mentioned in s.8

items: ==Appeal on conviction== available to higher courts — but ==no automatic stay==: disqualification applies even while appeal is pending ([[Lily Thomas v. UoI, 2013]]).
==Presidential disqualification (s.8A)==: no appeal, but a ==writ under Art 226 or 32== is possible.
==Against ECI decisions==: writ under Arts 226/32. The ==ECI can remove or reduce== the disqualification period on certain grounds (==s.11==).
==No bar to re-election== after the disqualification period.

head: Case
Holding
rows: Requires a ==nexus between gifts and voting inducement==, even via circumstantial evidence.
An appeal to vote based on the ==candidate's language== is a corrupt practice.
Promoting hatred ==against the government is not== a corrupt practice — only against ==classes of citizens== it is.
Struck down ==s.8(4)== — disqualification is ==immediate upon conviction==, even if appealed.
Disqualification applies for ==failure to disclose assets==.

items.title: Issues
bullets: ==No uniform standard of moral turpitude== under s.8 → selective application
==Delay in Presidential decisions== under s.8A — political bias possible
==Judicial review limitation== — courts review the outcome, not the procedure, in anti-defection cases
==Criminalisation of politics== — candidates contest until appeals are exhausted
==Politicisation== — disqualification weaponised for political gain

items.title: Global Best Practice
bullets: ==UK==: disqualification for those serving ==>1 year== in prison — ==no political discretion==
==Australia==: ==automatic disqualification== for offences with imprisonment >1 year; High Court supervises electoral disputes
==Philippines==: the electoral body has ==binding power to disqualify== candidates; clear timelines enforced

items.title: Way Forward
bullets: ==Time-bound decisions== — a fixed 3-month limit for Speaker and President
==Independent tribunal== for disqualification cases
==Automatic disqualification== for heinous offences without waiting for the political process
==Pre-screening of candidates== before nomination
==Greater ECI autonomy and binding powers==

items.title: Grounds — s.100
bullets: ==Corrupt practices== by candidate or agent
==Improper acceptance of nomination==
Improper use of ==official machinery==
Non-compliance with RoPA or Conduct Rules
Bribery, undue influence, ==booth capturing==, impersonation
==Result materially affected== by non-compliance or error

items.title: Procedure
bullets: Any ==elector or candidate== of the constituency may file
==Within 45 days== of result declaration (==s.81==)
Filed before the ==High Court== having jurisdiction (==s.80A==)
HC decision appealable to the ==SC (s.116A)==

items.title: Issues
bullets: ==Delays== — cases stretch for years, rendering them ==infructuous==
==High cost and complexity==
==No special benches or dedicated courts==
Political pressure on petitioners
==No fast-track mechanism==

head: Case
Holding
rows: Courts ==cannot interfere at intermediary stages== of the election process — only election petitions can challenge results.
==Strict compliance== with procedural requirements in election petitions.
Precedent for ==judicial review of election matters==; struck down the 39th Amendment.
The right to contest elections is ==not a fundamental right==.

items: ==Best practices==: ==UK== — petitions decided by the High Court with a strict ==21-day filing deadline==; ==Kenya== — a ==constitutionally mandated 6-month limit== to decide election petitions.

==Way forward==: ==public hearings== for transparency; reasonable costs to encourage genuine petitions; ==Election Tribunals== (II ARC, Ethics in Governance); a ==publicly available petition database==; ==penalty for frivolous petitions==.

blocks.text: The true test of a democratic state is not how elections are celebrated, but how transparently, fairly and swiftly they are regulated.
